summary: Four towers stood at Cape San Blas, Florida, from 1848; the 1885 iron tower was moved about twelve miles to Port St. Joe in 2014.

access.note: The tower stands in George Core Park, Port St. Joe. It can be climbed when open, for a fee; the grounds are free to visit.

events.note: Congress appropriated $8,000 for a tower at the cape's elbow (3 March 1847)
First tower completed April 1848; the nomination gives 85 feet, the Florida Lighthouse Association 65 feet, brick
First tower collapsed in a gale, 22-23 August 1851 (LighthouseFriends gives 23-24 August)
Second brick tower first lit, November 1855
Hurricane of 30 August 1856 destroyed the second tower
Third brick tower first lit 1 May 1859 with a third-order Fresnel lens
Civil War damage: keeper's dwelling destroyed; lens removed by the Confederate superintendent. The nomination does not date the damage, so the outbreak year is used
Returned to operation 23 July 1866 (the Florida Lighthouse Association gives 15 July)
Brick tower undermined, leaned and fell on 3 July 1882
A hurricane destroyed the station's dwelling about two months after the tower fell
Present iron skeleton tower; keepers' dwellings begun September 1884
Third-order lens first lit 30 June 1885
Gale of 8-9 October 1894 destroyed the keepers' dwellings and left the tower standing in water; the Board discontinued the light
Removal of the tower to Black's Island begun February 1896; stopped 30 April 1896 when the appropriation was used up
Board recommended reconstructing the light on the shell ridge, at a cost not exceeding $15,000
Sundry civil act of 6 June 1900 appropriated $15,000 for completing the removal to a new and safe site
Hurricane stripped the beach protecting the tower
Another storm left the tower 120 feet offshore
Tower moved a quarter mile inland; light discontinued 30 April 1918
Shown from the new site on 22 January 1919
Barge Holliswood lost off Cape San Blas in a storm on 23 May 1920; crew taken off by the tug Jim-Sid
LORAN radio station installed near the light
The nomination says the Coast Guard automated the light (the Florida Lighthouse Association gives 1972)
Light deactivated (the Florida Lighthouse Association gives 18 January 1996)
Hurricane Earl damaged the dwelling nearest the shore, two years after the deactivation
Both keepers' dwellings moved beside the tower; one restored that year, the second in 2005
Operations at the lighthouse shut down on 14 October 2012 (the nomination's date; it also gives 1996 as deactivation)
NPS letter of 21 December 2012: the City of Port St. Joe awarded the lighthouse; GSA transfer still to be made
Tower and dwellings moved about twelve miles to George Core Park, Port St. Joe, on 15 July 2014
Opened to the public 12 September 2014

corrections.why: The record's point is the tower's present site in George Core Park, Port St. Joe (moved there in July 2014). The light station stood on Cape San Blas from 1885 to 2014; the USLHS place gives the cape position to the minute (29.67167, -85.35667, approximate). A second record, us-fl-cape-san-blas-2, already carries the cape position.
1848 is the first brick tower, completed April 1848 and collapsed in 1851. The standing iron skeleton tower was built 1884-85 (first lit 30 June 1885).

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's first_lit 1847 (Rowlett: station established) is the year Congress authorised the tower. The nomination dates the first tower's completion to April 1848 and gives no first lighting date, so the research leaves first_lit out of the facts.

1996 is the deactivation date in the nomination and the Florida Lighthouse Association (18 January 1996). The nomination also says operations were shut down on 14 October 2012 and does not reconcile the two dates; the facts keep 1996.

notes_for_editor: Disagreements left open in the story, not settled: (1) the first tower's height: 85 feet in the nomination, 65 feet (brick) in the Florida Lighthouse Association; (2) the present tower's height: 96 feet in the nomination, 101 feet and a 98-foot focal height in the Association and USLHS (USLHS gives tower height 90 feet); (3) the 1851 collapse date (22-23 vs 23-24 August); (4) the 1866 relighting (23 vs 15 July); (5) automation 1981 (nomination) vs 1972 (Association), and electrification 1938 (Association only); (6) the keepers' dwellings: work finished February 1885 in the nomination's history, 1905 in its summary, a 1904 appropriation for new dwellings, and USLHS gives keepers' quarters 1919; (7) the Civil War damage: 'Southern troops' (nomination) vs 'the Confederate Army burned the keepers quarters' (Association); (8) the 1896-1900 removal: the Board reports describe a removal begun at Black's Island in 1896, $4,500 for completing it (1897) and $15,000 (1900); the nomination says the Board left the tower where it was and used $7,000 for dwellings in 1904. The story states both and does not reconcile them. (9) The lens: the Association gives a 1906 Barbier, Benard & Turenne bivalve lens; the nomination describes a third-order Fresnel lens of 1885 with a possible c.1905-06 origin for the present lens. Lens status and whether it is on display were not checked. (10) Visiting hours come from an undated visitor guide (Wednesday to Saturday, 11 to 5). The Association page still says climbing is on Friday and Saturday only. Check the lighthouse's own site before publication; it carried no hours in the text read. (11) Owner: the nomination says the City of Port St. Joe was awarded the lighthouse in 2012; the Association page still lists Eglin Air Force Base; the lighthouse website footer names the St. Joseph Historical Society as publisher. Confirm the current owner and operator. OCR and matching: the 1896, 1899 and 1900 Board entries were read from the OCR text (scan pages cited, printed page numbers not read; the Board volume's 'printed p.' is unknown). Quinn and Long were matched to the roster by name and office in the same reports. The 1899 report's distance for the shell ridge is garbled in OCR ('about If miles') and is not used. The 1871 Rousseau quotation and the 1856 and 1882 Board and Holland passages are read through the nomination, which quotes them; the originals were not read. The roster is printed as the archive gives it, spellings included (e.g. Francis Avrion, James R. Linton), and has not been checked against NARA registers. Keepers whose service ended after about 1960 appear in the roster only as the archive prints them and are not named in the story. Duplicate record: us-fl-cape-san-blas-2 holds the USLHS cape position and events 1849 first_lit, 1859 lens, 1885 built, 1996 deactivated; the editor should decide whether the two records merge. Linton's death is reported only as the nomination reports it, with the nomination's source. Please review that wording. No photos were added; the station record's Wikimedia Commons image was not checked. Fact-check 2026-10-27: footnote 11 (the $4,500 for completing the removal, approved 4 June 1897) is on scan 375, which lies after the fiscal 1897 report header at scan 245, so it is now cited as the year ended 30 June 1897; the Long reimbursement is cited to scan 144 only. The Florida Lighthouse Association's Friday-and-Saturday climbing days are now stated beside the visitor guide's Wednesday-to-Saturday hours. Open: the 1882 quotation is Francis Ross Holland's (Dover, 1988) as the nomination quotes it; that book was not read.
